source.author: verg
source.text: Hinc metuunt cupiuntque, dolent gaudentque, neque auras dispiciunt clausae tenebris et carcere caeco.
source.text_original: Hinc metuunt cupiuntque, dolent gaudentque, neque auras / dispiciunt clausae tenebris et carcere caeco.
source.text_english: From this they fear and desire, they grieve and rejoice, and do not discern the air, shut in by darkness and a blind prison.

reuse.author: hier
reuse.text: Audisse me memini quatuor perturbationes, de quibus plenissime Cicero in Tusculanis disputat, gaudii, aegritudinis, cupidinis et timoris, quorum duo praesentia, duo futura sunt, per quatuor significari animalia, de quibus et Virgilius breviter: Hinc metuunt, cupiuntque, dolent, gaudentque: quae regi debeant ratione, et potentia Dei; quibusque oppositae sint, immo impositae, virtutes quatuor, Prudentia, Justitia, Fortitudo, Temperantia, ut harum gubernentur arbitrio.
reuse.text_original: Audisse me memini quatuor perturbationes, de quibus plenissime Cicero in Tusculanis disputat, gaudii, aegritudinis, cupidinis et timoris, quorum duo praesentia, duo futura sunt, per quatuor significari animalia, de quibus et Virgilius breviter: Hinc metuunt, cupiuntque, dolent, gaudentque: quae regi debeant ratione, et potentia Dei; quibusque oppositae sint, immo impositae, virtutes quatuor, Prudentia, Justitia, Fortitudo, Temperantia, ut harum gubernentur arbitrio.
reuse.text_english: I remember having heard that the four disturbances, of which Cicero discusses most fully in the Tusculan Disputations—joy, distress, desire, and fear, of which two belong to the present and two to the future—are signified by the four living creatures, of which Virgil also says briefly: Hence they fear, desire, grieve, and rejoice. These are to be ruled by reason and by the power of God; and opposed to them, indeed set over against them, are the four virtues, Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance, so that they may be governed by their decision.
